name: McDougall starch diet

card.summary: A low-fat, plant-based diet built on starches such as rice, potatoes and corn, followed by people who want to lose body fat and improve skin and overall health.
card.aka: McDougall diet; McDougall Plan; The Starch Solution
card.note: Excludes all animal foods and added oils; critics raise concerns about nutrient gaps and protein.

quick.overview:
The McDougall diet is a very low-fat, high-carbohydrate eating plan developed by the American physician John McDougall. Roughly 90% of calories come from starches such as rice, potatoes, corn, bread and pasta, with fruit and vegetables, and no animal products or added oils [1].

Followers use it mainly to lean out and to improve general health markers, which feeds into how they look through lower body fat. Published research is mostly on health conditions such as multiple sclerosis and cholesterol rather than on appearance, and findings are described as limited and mixed [1][2][3].
quick.how: People eat unrefined starches and vegetables as the base of every meal, avoid meat, dairy, eggs, oils and processed foods, and in McDougall's programmes also limit alcohol, caffeine and sodium [1]. McDougall ran a 10-day residential programme in Santa Rosa, California, from 2002 [1].
quick.risks: Critics cite possible shortfalls in calcium, iron, protein and other nutrients, boredom, and gas from high fibre intake [1]. The American Heart Association scored the diet 73% aligned with its 2021 guidance, noting its exclusion of nuts, seeds and avocados conflicts with that guidance [1]. People with medical conditions typically consult a clinician before major changes.

lead: The McDougall diet, also called the McDougall Plan or starch solution, is a low-fat, vegan, starch-centred diet promoted by the American physician John A. McDougall (1947-2024), starting with his 1983 book The McDougall Plan [1].

Foods centre on rice, potatoes, corn, bread, pasta, fruit and vegetables, with about 90% of calories from starch, and it excludes animal products, added oils, processed foods, alcohol and caffeine [1]. Followers describe fat loss, a leaner look and clearer health markers as the payoff, and bodybuilding forums have discussed it as one of several high-carbohydrate approaches [4].

McDougall promoted it for arthritis, heart disease, diabetes, hypertension and other conditions [1]. Reviews of dietary patterns in multiple sclerosis discuss it among alternative diets and conclude that evidence is limited and trials small [2][3][5].

chain: Eat starch- and plant-based, very low fat
Lower calorie density and body fat
Leaner physique and improved health markers
angle.text: Followers use the diet to reduce body fat through low-calorie-density, high-fibre meals, which they connect to a leaner look. Appearance effects come through weight change rather than through any direct action on skin or features.

infobox: Animal products, added oils, processed foods [1]

paras: The plan centres on starches, supplemented by fruits and vegetables. It is very low in fat and high in carbohydrate and fibre, and it restricts sodium [1]. McDougall's later books include The McDougall Program for Maximum Weight Loss (1995) and The Starch Solution (2012) [1].

A review of diet patterns in multiple sclerosis lists the McDougall diet among alternative models and notes small, short, often non-blinded human trials, concluding that insufficient evidence exists to recommend any specific diet for the condition [2][5]. One study of the diet in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis reported no change in MRI, relapses or disability [1]. Other reports describe lower LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, insulin and BMI among followers [1].
Commentators describe the plan as a low-fat diet with health claims that exceed the trial evidence, while noting its emphasis on whole grains, fruit and vegetables resembles mainstream advice [1].

On training forums the diet comes up in discussions of high-carbohydrate, low-fat eating and vegan muscle gain, where participants debate whether carbohydrate-heavy approaches suit lean-physique goals [4].

Human research is limited to small studies, mostly in people with multiple sclerosis, where reviews describe the trials as small and non-blinded [2][3][5]. No trials have tested its effect on appearance.

timeline.event: The McDougall Plan is published and becomes a bestseller [1].
The McDougall Program for Maximum Weight Loss appears [1].
McDougall starts a 10-day residential programme in Santa Rosa, California [1].
